question: The speed of sound in air depends on:
explanation: p/ρ = RT, so pressure and density enter only through their ratio. At constant temperature a is unchanged at any altitude.

question: Flight regimes by free-stream Mach number are conventionally:

options.text: Subsonic below about 0.75, transonic about 0.75–1.2, supersonic 1.2–5, hypersonic above 5

explanation: Transonic flow contains both subsonic and supersonic regions; its bounds depend on the body, not on M = 1 exactly.

question: Compressibility is usually neglected below M ≈ 0.3 because:

options.text: The speed of sound is infinite
Stagnation density exceeds free-stream density by under 5 %

question: At M 0.8, the ratio of total to static pressure is:
At M 0.8, impact pressure q_c = p_t − p exceeds the incompressible dynamic pressure q = 0.7pM² by about:
explanation: q_c/q = [(1.128)^3.5 − 1]/(0.7 × 0.64) = 1.170 (≈ 1 + M²/4 + M⁴/40). This is the compressibility error the CAS → EAS correction removes.

question: Dynamic pressure in terms of Mach number is q = 0.7·p·M². At FL350 (p = 23,840 Pa) and M 0.80, q is:
W/S = 5,500 N/m² at FL350 (p = 23,840 Pa), M 0.78. The cruise CL is:
At constant weight and Mach number, climbing to a lower static pressure requires:

options.text: A higher CL in proportion to √p
A higher CL, in inverse proportion to pressure

explanation: L = 0.7·p·M²·S·CL. At fixed W and M, CL ∝ 1/p — a key reason high-altitude flight approaches buffet limits.

question: The Prandtl–Glauert factor 1/√(1 − M²) at M 0.6 and M 0.8 is:
Below the critical Mach number, increasing M at constant α changes the section lift coefficient by:
explanation: Linearised subsonic theory scales all Cp, hence cl and lift-curve slope, by the Prandtl–Glauert factor.

question: A pressure coefficient of −0.43 at low speed becomes, at M 0.6 (below critical):
The critical Mach number is:

options.text: The free-stream Mach number at which local flow first reaches M = 1 somewhere on the body
The Mach number at which drag rises sharply

explanation: Local acceleration over the upper surface reaches sonic speed below free-stream M = 1; supersonic pockets and shocks form above it.

question: A section's minimum incompressible pressure coefficient is −0.6. Using Prandtl–Glauert scaling and the sonic-Cp relation, its critical Mach number is closest to:
explanation: Solve −0.6/√(1 − M²) = Cp*(M): at M 0.69 both are ≈ −0.83. A stronger suction peak (Cp₀ −1.0) gives about 0.61.

question: The sonic pressure coefficient Cp* (the Cp at which local M = 1) at free-stream M 0.8 is about:
Critical Mach number is increased by:

options.text: Thinner sections, less camber, lower CL and sweepback

explanation: All reduce the peak local velocity (or its normal component); lower super-velocity reaches sonic at higher free-stream M.

question: At high altitude (higher cruise CL), the critical Mach number is:

options.text: Lower, because higher α increases the upper-surface suction peak

explanation: M_crit falls with CL; heavy aircraft at high altitude reach shock formation at a lower Mach number.

question: Above the critical Mach number but below drag divergence:

options.text: A small supersonic region terminated by a weak shock exists, with little drag rise

explanation: The shock is initially weak and near the suction peak; drag rises steeply only when it strengthens and moves aft, triggering separation (drag divergence Mach).

question: Drag divergence Mach number is:

options.text: The Mach number at which drag begins to rise steeply (e.g. dCD/dM = 0.1)

explanation: It lies somewhat above M_crit; supercritical sections widen the gap.

question: Sweep raises the critical Mach number because:

options.text: Pressure distribution depends mainly on the velocity component normal to the leading edge, M·cos Λ

explanation: Simple sweep theory: the spanwise component does not accelerate over the section.

question: Free-stream M 0.85, sweep 35°. The normal Mach component is:
To keep the normal Mach component at 0.70 when cruising at M 0.85, the sweep must be about:
A straight wing with M_crit 0.70 is swept 30°. Simple sweep theory predicts M_crit:
explanation: M_crit/cos Λ = 0.70/0.866 = 0.81. Root and tip effects and finite span reduce the real gain.

question: Disadvantages of sweep include:

options.text: Lower lift slope and CLmax, tip stall and pitch-up, spanwise flow and higher structural weight

explanation: Lift ∝ cos Λ effect, tip-loaded flow and longer, more twisted structure are the costs of higher M_crit.

question: Swept-wing lift-curve slope is approximately the unswept value times:
explanation: Only the normal velocity component contributes; at 35° the slope falls to 0.82 of the straight-wing value.

question: A supercritical aerofoil achieves a higher drag-divergence Mach number by:

options.text: A flatter upper surface with lower, more uniform suction and a weak shock, plus aft camber for lift

explanation: Flatter upper-surface curvature limits local Mach number ahead of a weak shock; aft loading recovers lift. It allows thicker wings at the same cruise Mach.

question: The transonic area rule states that wave drag is minimised when:

options.text: The total cross-sectional area distribution along the aircraft varies smoothly

explanation: Abrupt area growth at the wing junction causes strong shocks; waisting the fuselage or adding fairings smooths the distribution.

question: Thin wings are used on high-speed aircraft mainly because:

options.text: They raise the critical and drag-divergence Mach numbers

explanation: Lower thickness reduces super-velocity; the cost is lower CLmax and less structural depth.

question: Vortex generators on transonic wings are used to:

options.text: Energise the boundary layer ahead of the shock, reducing shock-induced separation

explanation: Mixing supplies momentum to withstand the pressure jump across the shock, reducing buffet and drag.

question: Climbing at constant CAS (300 kt) in the standard atmosphere, Mach number:

options.text: Increases until the tropopause, then decreases

explanation: Constant impact pressure over falling static pressure raises q_c/p and hence M; falling temperature reduces a as well.

question: The crossover altitude for a 300 kt CAS / M 0.80 climb schedule is about:
explanation: Solving M(CAS 300, altitude) = 0.80 in the standard atmosphere gives ≈ 30,600 ft; above it the Mach limit governs.

question: At the 300 kt / M 0.80 crossover altitude, the TAS is about:
Above the crossover altitude, speed limitations are expressed as MMO rather than VMO because:

options.text: Compressibility effects (Mach-dependent) become the limiting factor before dynamic-pressure limits

explanation: At high altitude a given CAS corresponds to a high Mach number; shock effects are Mach-driven.

question: Descending at constant Mach number from above the tropopause into the troposphere, CAS:

options.text: Increases throughout, and TAS increases in the troposphere as temperature rises

explanation: Higher static pressure at the same M increases q_c; rising temperature raises a and TAS.

question: W/S = 5,000 N/m² at FL410 (p = 17,870 Pa). If buffet onset CL is 0.6, the minimum Mach for 1 g flight is about:
explanation: M = √((W/S)/(0.7·p·CL)) = √(5,000/7,507) = 0.816. A 1.3 g margin requires M 0.93 — the coffin-corner squeeze.

question: With the same data (W/S 5,000, FL410, CL_buffet 0.6), a 1.3 g buffet margin requires a minimum Mach of about:
explanation: √(1.3 × 5,000/7,507) = 0.93. If MMO or high-speed buffet is below this, the altitude is too high for that weight.

question: The coffin corner is the altitude at which:

options.text: Low-speed (stall/buffet) and high-speed (Mach buffet) limits converge

explanation: Low-speed buffet Mach rises with altitude (higher CL); high-speed buffet Mach is roughly constant or falls. The margin vanishes where they meet.

question: Increasing weight at constant altitude affects the buffet margin by:

options.text: Raising the low-speed buffet Mach and lowering the available margin

explanation: CL required ∝ W; low-speed buffet occurs at a higher M. The buffet-limited ceiling falls with weight.

question: The Mach meter indicates Mach number from:
explanation: M = f(q_c/p) through the isentropic relation; no temperature input is needed.

question: At constant altitude and TAS in warmer air, the Mach meter reading:

options.text: Decreases, because the speed of sound is higher

explanation: M = TAS/a and a ∝ √T.

question: At constant pressure altitude and constant CAS, a temperature increase leaves Mach number:

options.text: Unchanged, since M depends only on q_c and p

explanation: CAS fixes q_c; altitude fixes p. TAS rises with √T and so does a, in the same ratio.

question: Air at M 0.8 and T = 217 K is brought to rest adiabatically. Total temperature is about:
A total-air-temperature probe with recovery factor 1 reads 245 K at M 0.8. Static air temperature is:
Kinetic heating of the skin is a design constraint mainly at:

options.text: High altitude only at low speed
Supersonic speeds, where stagnation temperature rises steeply with M²

explanation: At M 2 and 217 K, T_t = 217 × 1.8 = 391 K, affecting material strength.

question: The Mach angle μ for M 2 is:
explanation: μ = arcsin(1/M) = arcsin 0.5 = 30°. At M 1.414, μ = 45°.

question: In supersonic flow through a diverging passage, the flow:
explanation: dA/A = (M² − 1)dV/V: for M > 1, area and velocity increase together.

question: Supersonic thin-aerofoil theory gives a lift-curve slope of 4/√(M² − 1) per radian. At M 2 it is:
explanation: 4/√3 = 2.31 — below the subsonic 2π, and falling with M.

question: In supersonic flow, disturbances from a body:

options.text: Are instantly felt throughout the flow
Cannot propagate upstream beyond the Mach cone
Travel slower than in subsonic flow

explanation: The flow speed exceeds the propagation speed; the zone of influence is confined within the Mach cone, so the flow meets the body unwarned — hence shocks.

question: A sharp leading edge is used on supersonic wings because:

options.text: It allows an attached oblique shock with lower wave drag than a detached bow shock

explanation: A blunt nose forces a detached normal-shock segment with large total-pressure loss; the price is poor low-speed stall behaviour.

question: A subsonic leading edge on a highly swept supersonic wing is one for which:

options.text: The Mach number normal to the leading edge is below 1 (leading edge inside the Mach cone)

explanation: M·cos Λ < 1 allows rounded, subsonic-type leading-edge flow and lower wave drag.

question: Doubling TAS at constant temperature changes the Mach number by:
explanation: M = V/a; a depends on temperature only.

question: At FL400 in the standard atmosphere, 450 kt TAS corresponds to about:
The ratio of impact pressure to dynamic pressure, q_c/q, as Mach number rises from 0.3 to 0.8:
Near and above the critical Mach number, Prandtl–Glauert scaling:

options.text: Becomes invalid, since the flow contains shocks and is no longer linear

explanation: It assumes small, isentropic, subsonic perturbations everywhere.

question: Increasing wing thickness for more fuel volume at the same cruise Mach is possible with:

options.text: A conventional section and less sweep
A supercritical section and adequate sweep

explanation: The supercritical design delays drag divergence, recovering Mach capability that thickness would cost.

question: Critical Mach number of the complete aircraft is often set by:

options.text: The component with the highest local velocity: wing upper surface, wing–body junction, nacelles or canopy

explanation: Any local super-velocity reaching sonic defines M_crit; junction fairings and area ruling address this.

question: The maximum operating Mach number MMO protects against:

options.text: Shock-induced buffet, control problems (e.g. Mach tuck) and drag rise

explanation: VMO protects against q-related loads and flutter; MMO against compressibility effects.

question: At constant altitude, increasing speed from M 0.75 to 0.82 on a transport wing usually:

options.text: Increases drag disproportionately as drag divergence is approached

explanation: Wave drag and shock-induced separation add to the q-based drag rise.

question: The transonic range is aerodynamically difficult mainly because:

options.text: Mixed subsonic and supersonic regions and moving shocks cause large, non-linear changes in lift, drag and moments

explanation: Local shock positions shift with small changes in M or α, producing buffet, trim changes and control effectiveness loss.

question: At the same critical Mach number, sweep allows:

options.text: A thicker section, improving structure and fuel volume

explanation: M_n = M·cos Λ; the section only needs to meet M_crit at the normal component.

question: In subsonic compressible flow, the local density at the upper-surface suction peak compared with free stream is:
explanation: Acceleration lowers pressure and, isentropically, density — the effect grows with M.

question: An aircraft cruising at constant Mach number climbs from FL310 to FL370 (both below or near the tropopause). Its IAS:
explanation: At constant M the impact pressure falls with static pressure, so CAS/IAS falls.

question: Ram temperature rise at M 0.5 and T 250 K is about:
Two sections at the same CL: A has t/c 10 %, B has t/c 14 %. Section A's critical Mach number is:
explanation: Thicker sections accelerate the flow more; sonic conditions arise at a lower free-stream M.

question: The wave drag of a slender supersonic body is reduced by:

options.text: High fineness ratio and smooth area distribution

explanation: Wave drag depends on the second derivative of the area distribution; long, smooth shapes minimise it.

question: Wing-body fairings on transonic aircraft reduce:

options.text: Local super-velocities and interference shocks at the junction

explanation: The junction combines fuselage and wing velocity increments; fairing shape keeps local M below that giving strong shocks.

question: Buffet onset boundary charts are used to determine:

options.text: The maximum altitude or bank at a given weight and Mach number while keeping a load-factor margin to buffet

explanation: They plot buffet CL against M; with W, p and n the margin can be read directly.

question: The local Mach number at a point on the wing depends on:
explanation: Acceleration also cools the air (isentropic expansion), lowering local a — both raise local M.

question: The subsonic compressibility effect on the aerodynamic centre position is:

options.text: Small, with the AC staying near the quarter chord until shocks form
A shift to mid-chord at M 0.3
A forward shift to the leading edge

explanation: Prandtl–Glauert scales the whole Cp distribution; its centroid moves little. Aft AC movement comes with shocks.

question: Flying at constant CAS above the crossover altitude would:
explanation: At constant CAS, M continues to rise with altitude.

question: TAT exceeds SAT in flight because:

options.text: The probe brings the air (partly) to rest, converting kinetic energy into enthalpy

explanation: Recovery factor r gives TAT = SAT(1 + 0.2rM²).
